Here is the itemized extraction of every place where Pieter K. Baaij expresses uncertainty, discusses competing textual forms, notes Hebrew/Greek ambiguities, allows authorial adaptation, disagrees with other scholars, or acknowledges weakening evidence in Paulus als Schriftuitlegger: Paulus’ vertolking van Genesis 15:5b-6 in Romeinen 4:3.
1. B001-1: Romans 4:3 / Genesis 15:6
A. Expresses Uncertainty / Explicit Assumptions
Assumption Regarding Masoretic Text Identity: Baaij explicitly acknowledges that his entire exegetical reconstruction relies on the assumption that Paul's Hebrew Vorlage did not deviate from today's Masoretic Text:
Quote / Summary: "Hierbij gaan wij ervan uit dat, wat deze passage aangaat, de Hebreeuwse tekst die Paulus heeft gekend, niet heeft afgeweken van de Hebreeuwse tekst die ons ter beschikking staat, namelijk de Masoretische tekst" [Section 1, Passage 13].
Acknowledging Translation Limitations ("Traduttore Traditore"): Baaij notes that even when applying Paul's own linguistic tools, all translation inherently involves a degree of distortion:
Quote / Summary: "Niettemin blijft, zelfs onder de door mij genoemde voorwaarden, vertalen toch een vorm van verraden (‘traduttore tradittore’)..." [Section 4, Passage 36].
B. Discusses Competing Textual Forms
Hebrew Masoretic Text vs. Septuagint (LXX): Baaij analyzes the divergence between MT Genesis 15:6 (waw + hif'il verb 'āman followed by ḥāšaḇ) and LXX Genesis 15:6 (καὶ ἐπίστευσεν Ἀβρὰμ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐλογίσθη αὐτῷ εἰς δικαιοσύνην). He notes that the LXX places the name "Abram" first and uses passive constructions that obscure Hebrew syntax [Section 3, Passages 20, 27].
Polemic Against Septuagint Misleading Readers: Baaij asserts that relying on LXX renderings leads translators to teach the opposite of Hebrew Scripture:
Quote / Summary: "De LXX, stelt Paulus, leert de mens het tegenovergestelde van wat de Schrift zegt (Baaij, 2003:145-148)" [Section 5, Passages 43–45].
Comparison with Dutch Translation Traditions: Baaij systematically compares Romans 4:3 and Genesis 15:6 across the Statenvertaling, NBG-vertaling (1951), Willibrord-vertaling (1995), and Nieuwe Bijbelvertaling (NBV, 2004), demonstrating how all four misplace the grammatical emphasis by putting "Abram / Abraham" at the beginning of the clause rather than highlighting the active verb "trusted" (ἐπίστευσεν) [Section 2, Passages 17–19; Section 5, Passage 37].
Rejection of Rabbinic / Midrashic Interpretation: Baaij explicitly notes that the rabbinic/midrashic exegesis developed in Persian and Hellenistic times (later codified in Midrash) is rejected by Paul in Romans as taking human possession of Scripture [Section 2, Passage 15].
C. Notes Hebrew / Greek Ambiguity & Semantic Nuances
Translation Ambiguity of Hebrew 'āman (Hif'il): Citing Jepsen (ThWAT I, 320), Baaij notes that the hif'il of 'āman is difficult to render into Dutch ("moeilijk in onze taal weer te geven"). He evaluates proposed German renderings (Fest sein, Festigkeit hebben/gewinnen) and defines it as an inner-transitive active response of trust to a divine Initiator ("zich toevertrouwen aan") [Section 3, Passage 23].
Semantic Nuances of Hebrew ḥāšaḇ: Citing Seybold (ThWAT III, 246–248), Baaij notes the dual aspects of ḥāšaḇ ("counting/calculating" vs. "planning/designing/choosing"), emphasizing that attribution proceeds solely from prior divine knowledge [Section 3, Passage 24].
Nuance of ṣəḏāqāh vs. ṣædæq: Citing Johnson (ThWAT VI, 916) and Van Dorp (2004), Baaij distinguishes ṣəḏāqāh (active, restorative activity re-establishing a relationship) from static principle (ṣædæq), translating it as "rechtschapenheid" ("herstel van de relatie tussen God en de door Hem aangesproken mens") [Section 3, Passages 25–26].
Grammatical Ambiguity of πιστεύω Constructions: Baaij contrasts πιστεύω constructed with a simple dative (τῷ θεῷ) in Romans 4:3 as a dativus causae (highlighting God as Initiator/Cause) with πιστεύω ἐπί cum dativo (Rom 9:33; 10:11) and πιστεύω εἰς cum accusativo (Rom 4:5, 24) [Section 3, Passage 30].
Passive λογίζομαι with εἰς: Baaij notes that Paul uses a passive form of λογίζομαι with εἰς to translate Hebrew ḥāšaḇ, where εἰς literally means "towards" ("naar... toe") to stress that righteousness is an unmerited gift from God [Section 3, Passage 33].
D. Allows Authorial Adaptation & Non-Literal Translation
Intentional Dynamic Re-translation: Baaij explicitly states that Paul does not translate the Hebrew text literally, but adapts his Greek phrasing to capture the original author's exact intent:
Quote / Summary: "Paulus volgt de grondtekst niet letterlijk, maar geeft de inhoud ervan weer... Paulus wil door zijn weergave duidelijker aangeven waar het de bijbelschrijver om gaat" [Section 3, Passage 33].
Specific Authorial Modifications:
Placing ἐπίστευσεν first with postpositive δέ to emphasize active trust [Section 3, Passage 29].
Inserting τῷ θεῷ as a dativus causae [Section 3, Passage 30].
Replacing the Septuagint's "Abram" (Ἀβράμ) with the covenant name "Abraham" (Ἀβραάμ) [Section 3, Passage 30].
E. Disagrees with Other Scholars
C. E. B. Cranfield (1985) & Joseph A. Fitzmyer (1993): Disagrees with their assertion that Paul must be understood through Hellenistic-Roman culture, maintaining (via W. C. van Unnik) that Paul thought in Biblical Hebrew out of a Pharisaic Jerusalem upbringing [Section 1, Footnote 3, Passages 8, 11, 13].
E. P. Meijering (2003): Disagrees with Meijering’s claim that Paul quoted Scripture selectively and intervened in or altered Old Testament texts to suit his theology [Section 3, Footnote 8, Passage 32].
C. J. den Heijer (1998): Disagrees with Den Heijer’s characterization of Romans 3:20b and 3:21 as "very negative statements about the Torah", proving that Den Heijer relied on flawed Dutch translations rather than Paul's Hebrew-grounded Greek [Section 5, Passages 38–41].
J. van Bruggen (2001): Disagrees with Van Bruggen’s exegetical explanations that rely on Hellenistic Greek assumptions or existing translations [Section 5, Footnote 9, Passage 41].
Translators of Dutch Bible Versions: Disagrees with the translators of the Statenvertaling, NBG 1951, Willibrord 1995, and NBV 2004 for misinterpreting Genesis 15:6 and Romans 4:3 [Section 2, Passages 17–19; Section 5, Passage 37].
F. Acknowledges Evidence Weakening Preferred Interpretation
Falsification Condition on Hebrew Text: Baaij explicitly states that if Paul's Hebrew text differed from the Masoretic Text (BHS), his entire grammatical argument would be invalidated:
Quote / Summary: "Hierbij gaan wij ervan uit dat... de Hebreeuwse tekst die Paulus heeft gekend, niet heeft afgeweken van... de Masoretische tekst" [Section 1, Passage 13].
2. B001-4: Romans 10:11 / Isaiah 28:16
Page / Locator: Section 3, Passage 30.
Discusses Competing Textual / Prepositional Forms: Baaij explicitly contrasts Paul's use of πιστεύω with a simple dative (τῷ θεῷ) in Romans 4:3 with his use of πιστεύω ἐπί with the dative in Romans 10:11 (and Romans 9:33) (πιστεύω ἐπ' αὐτῷ), noting that in Romans 10:11 the preposition ἐπί shifts the grammatical focus to the divine object of faith [Section 3, Passage 30].
